name: Samsung Keyboard
scope_note: Scoped as a brief pass for UX patterns only, per the research brief. Samsung Keyboard is closed source, OEM-locked to Galaxy devices, and has no published theme format for the keyboard itself. Its value as a reference is the UNUSUAL PRODUCT SHAPE: Samsung deliberately keeps the stock keyboard's built-in theming minimal and pushes all real customization into three separate downloadable companion apps (Galaxy Themes, Theme Park, Keys Cafe). Technical internals are inferred throughout and flagged accordingly.
evidence_basis: Samsung official support pages, Samsung Developer / Galaxy Themes Studio documentation, and hands-on coverage of the Good Lock modules (XDA, Android Police, Pocket-lint). No format documentation exists for keyboard theme internals.
rendering_approach: Per-key drawing is the primary model, which is the key structural difference from Gboard and SwiftKey. Stock Samsung Keyboard themes (Light, Solid light, Dark, Solid dark, Color palette) are pure color-token themes with no image layer at all - Theme Park's keyboard editor lets you set the keyboard background color and then style INDIVIDUAL KEY GROUPS separately (letter keys, number keys, and function keys are each independently colored), plus the key-press effect, which only makes sense if each key owns its own drawable. Samsung Keyboard notably does NOT support a photo background natively - Samsung's own support answer is to install a separate app. Where image backgrounds do exist they arrive via two companion routes: Keys Cafe's 'Style your own keyboard' can place a Gallery image as the keyboard background (whole-image paste behind the key layer), and Theme Park lets you set keycaps and text to 'your own color OR image', which is per-key image fill rather than a single background paste - a notably different and more granular model than the Gboard/SwiftKey single-photo approach. Samsung developer material also notes 'Samsung Keyboard keys can have images now' for Galaxy Themes designers. So Samsung spans all three modes: per-key color (stock), per-key image (Theme Park / Galaxy Themes), and whole-image background (Keys Cafe). [uncertain - the per-key vs whole-image split is inferred from the editors' control surfaces and from screenshots, not from any published rendering documentation]
selector_and_state_model: No public rule syntax. What the editors expose implies a role-plus-state slot map similar in spirit to SwiftKey's: KEY ROLES are explicitly and separately addressable - Theme Park styles letter keys, number keys, and function keys as three distinct groups with independent color/image, which is the most explicitly role-segmented consumer control surface of the three keyboards researched. STATES: a 'key-press effect' is a first-class settable property in Theme Park, and Keys Cafe adds per-key-press color effects and animations, so pressed state is genuinely themeable rather than merely implied. Keys Cafe additionally exposes LAYOUT-level targeting that no other keyboard here offers - individual keys can be added, removed, reordered, and repositioned, and function keys, special characters, emoji, frequently-used words and kaomoji can be assigned to specific key slots, meaning the addressable unit descends to the individual key rather than stopping at the role. Not evidenced: shift/caps-state-specific art, disabled state, focus state, or any declarative selector language. Underneath, Galaxy Themes are Android RRO-style resource overlays, so the real 'selector' is Android resource-name overriding - you replace the drawable or color the keyboard app already references by name. [uncertain - the RRO/resource-name-overriding characterization is inferred from Samsung's overlay theme architecture and community overlay work, not confirmed for the keyboard specifically]
rendering_pipeline: Android View/Canvas/Drawable inside an InputMethodService, consistent with every other production Android IME; no evidence of Jetpack Compose. Samsung Keyboard (Honeyboard) is a system app on One UI, so it can additionally consume Samsung's private theme framework via the Theme Center service in ways a third-party keyboard cannot - notably it can be restyled by a system-wide theme package without shipping its own theme engine. Per-keystroke cost is the usual invalidate-touched-key-rect pattern, with the caveat that Keys Cafe's key-press animations and effects add per-press animation work that plain color themes do not. Samsung's keyboard has a public reputation for sluggishness relative to Gboard, with One UI 8 coverage framing keyboard responsiveness as something users must tune via settings. [uncertain - entirely inferred; Samsung publishes no architecture detail for Honeyboard]
compositing_scrim_model: This is the weakest area of the Samsung reference and a genuine gap: there is NO documented brightness or dimming scrim for keyboard background images, on any of the three routes. Because stock Samsung theming is color-token based rather than photo based, the scrim problem never had to be solved in the core product, and neither Keys Cafe nor Theme Park is documented as offering a Gboard/SwiftKey-style brightness slider over a chosen image. Legibility over an image is instead handled by the per-key layer: because keys keep their own colored backgrounds, labels sit on a controlled surface rather than on raw photo pixels, which removes much of the need for a scrim. Two adjacent controls do exist and are worth noting: a TRANSPARENCY control that Samsung documents as available ONLY in floating keyboard mode (adjusting the keyboard's own alpha over the app behind it - the inverse of a background scrim, and an interesting UX pattern in its own right), and the High Contrast Keyboard accessibility mode described below. Anyone using Samsung as a reference should note that it solves the photo-legibility problem by NOT relying on a photo layer, rather than by dimming one. [uncertain - the absence of a brightness/scrim control in Keys Cafe and Theme Park is a negative finding from documentation and hands-on coverage that never mentions one; a build may have added it without coverage]
asset_types: Standard Android drawable resources - raster PNG (including 9-patch for stretchable key caps) and XML color/shape/state-list drawables, resolved through the normal density-bucket ladder, packaged inside a theme APK. Galaxy Themes Studio is explicitly a no-code visual tool that compiles designer artwork into an APK, so the assets are whatever the tool bakes into that APK's resource table. User-supplied images arrive as plain rasters from the Gallery (Keys Cafe background, Theme Park source image for color extraction and for key fills). No vector-only, Lottie, or video theme assets are evidenced, though Keys Cafe's key-press animations are presumably code-driven effects rather than declared assets. [uncertain - specific asset formats inside a Samsung keyboard theme are inferred from Android norms and the APK output format, not documented]
theme_package_manifest_format: No public schema for keyboard theme internals. What IS documented sits one level up, at the Galaxy Themes system-theme layer: a Samsung theme is an ANDROID APK, produced by Galaxy Themes Studio (a no-code design tool that 'create[s] it as an APK file'), signed, and installed through the Galaxy Themes / Theme Center service (com.samsung.android.themecenter, signed with the Samsung certificate CN=Samsung Cert, O=Samsung Corporation). The keyboard is one component inside that whole-system theme package alongside lock screen, home screen, dialer, contacts, messages, settings and icons - it is not an independently packaged artifact. The community overlay scene shows the same content can be delivered as Android runtime resource overlays (RRO) dropped into /system/vendor/overlay with correct permissions, or as regular installable overlay APKs, and third-party Samsung theme tooling generates 'ready-to-compile APK folders', compiles them, places the APKs into theme assets and emits an assets.txt that is pasted into a themes.json - so there IS a JSON index at the packaging/tooling layer, but that is community tooling convention, not a Samsung-published schema. Net: APK-based, signed, system-theme-scoped, no per-keyboard manifest format, nothing to copy directly. The separate Keys Cafe and Theme Park keyboard styles are stored by those apps in their own private formats with no documentation at all. [uncertain - themes.json/assets.txt is community tooling; the RRO characterization is inferred; Keys Cafe/Theme Park storage format is entirely unknown]
token_count_tiering: A pronounced and deliberately fragmented tiering, which is the most interesting UX lesson from Samsung. TIER 0 - stock, in-settings: essentially 1 control, a theme picker with 5 presets (Light, Solid light, Dark, Solid dark, Color palette), plus adjacent non-theme controls (keyboard size/position, font size slider, number row on/off, alternative characters, high contrast mode). No background image, no per-key color. TIER 1 - Theme Park: roughly 5-8 keyboard tokens - background color, letter-key color, number-key color, function-key color, key text color, key-press effect, with color or image accepted for keycaps and text, all seeded from an auto-extracted palette. TIER 2 - Keys Cafe: the deepest consumer tier of any keyboard researched, adding background image, per-key color effects, key-press animations, key SOUNDS, keyboard height/width/position, and full key layout editing (add/remove/reorder keys). TIER 3 - Galaxy Themes Studio: professional, approved-designers-only, whole-system theme authoring. Samsung's choice to put tiers 1-3 behind separate downloads rather than in the keyboard's own settings is a real product decision with a real cost - most users never find them, and Samsung's own support answer to 'how do I change my keyboard background' is 'install two more apps from Galaxy Store'. [uncertain - the Theme Park and Keys Cafe control counts are enumerated from hands-on coverage and may drift between module versions]
theme_versioning_forward_compat: Not documented for keyboard theming. Structurally, versioning is handled the way Android handles it for any APK: a theme is an installed, versioned, signed package, and the Galaxy Themes Service itself is versioned in lockstep with the Android release (distinct builds for Android 10, 11, 12, 15, 16), which implies the theme contract is re-baselined per platform version rather than carrying a forward-compatible schema. Practical consequence users report is the familiar one: themes and Good Lock modules break across One UI major upgrades and must be updated by their authors. Unknown-property handling is undefined because there is no property document. [uncertain - inferred from the per-Android-version Theme Service builds and general Good Lock upgrade breakage; no versioning documentation exists]
color_extraction_dynamic_tinting: Samsung's strongest and most directly relevant capability, and the best of the three items on this axis. Theme Park is built around DYNAMIC COLOR EXTRACTION: the user picks an image (typically their wallpaper), crops it, and the app 'extracts dominant colors' and automatically generates a full theme from them, including a keyboard theme, with a preview before applying. The extracted palette then drives the separately-colorable letter/number/function key groups. This is a full extract-then-map pipeline exposed as a consumer feature, and it is a closer match to what a photo-theme product usually wants than Gboard's approach, because Gboard's Dynamic Color consumes the OS palette and Gboard's photo path deliberately does no extraction at all. Separately, One UI's own 'Color palette' keyboard theme and system-wide wallpaper-derived theming give a Material-You-equivalent path on modern One UI. Stock preset themes remain pre-baked. The transferable pattern: crop -> extract dominant colors -> map onto a small set of role tokens -> preview -> apply. [uncertain - the specific extraction algorithm (Palette API vs Samsung's own) is not documented]
contrast_enforcement_accessibility: No evidence of automated WCAG/APCA validation of composited output, but Samsung ships the strongest FIRST-PARTY ACCESSIBILITY ESCAPE HATCH of the three keyboards. 'High contrast keyboard' is a dedicated toggle under Settings > General management > Keyboard settings, part of Samsung's vision-enhancement accessibility features, and it offers FOUR contrast options rather than a single on/off - it 'uses brighter colours with a higher contrast background to help the keys stand out'. That is a real, shipped, multi-level high-contrast mode owned by the OS accessibility surface rather than by the theme system, which is an important architectural point: the accessibility override sits ABOVE the theme and can rescue any theme the user has applied, including a badly chosen image-based one. Samsung also ships a keyboard font-size slider, and the per-key-color model itself is inherently more legible over imagery than transparent keys are. What is missing: no brightness/scrim control, no automatic legibility computation, no warning when a user picks an unreadable color combination in Theme Park or Keys Cafe. Design lesson worth carrying: pair whatever theming you ship with a theme-independent high-contrast override that the user can reach from system accessibility settings, not just from your app. [uncertain - the four-contrast-option detail comes from support/press coverage and may vary by One UI version; the absence of validation in the editors is a negative finding]
background_geometry_adaptation: Samsung has the most geometry configurations to survive of the three, and correspondingly the least documentation about how art adapts to them. Documented modes: standard, one-handed, and floating, with INDEPENDENT MODE SELECTION FOR PORTRAIT AND LANDSCAPE (a nice UX detail - the user is not forced into one choice across orientations); floating turns the keyboard into a small draggable popup with its own transparency control; split mode divides the keyboard in half in landscape and on wide devices including tablets and Z Fold foldables; and the keyboard can be freely dragged and resized. Foldables make this materially harder than on a normal phone - the same theme must render on a narrow cover display and a large unfolded inner display and survive the fold transition. Because the dominant theme model is per-key COLOR rather than a positioned image, almost all of this is free: colors reflow with the layout at any size, which is precisely why a color-token model is the robust choice for a device family with this much geometry variance. The image-based routes (Keys Cafe background, Theme Park key images) inherit the usual scaling problem and have no documented crop or fit behavior. Take-away: Samsung's geometry robustness is a consequence of avoiding positioned imagery, not of solving image adaptation. [uncertain - no documentation exists on how Keys Cafe or Theme Park images scale across split/floating/foldable configurations]
layout_locale_independence: Robust, again as a consequence of the color-token model - per-key colors reflow to any key count, so the number row toggle, alternative-characters setting, non-QWERTY and non-Latin layouts across Samsung's wide language support, RTL locales, and split layouts all just work without per-layout theme variants. Keys Cafe complicates this in an interesting way: because it permits actual LAYOUT EDITING (adding, removing, reordering and repositioning keys), a Keys Cafe creation is partly a layout artifact rather than purely a skin, so it is inherently bound to the layout it was authored against in a way a pure theme is not - a custom key arrangement does not meaningfully transfer to a different script's layout. The whole-image background route is layout-independent for the same reason it is everywhere else: no per-key registration. [uncertain - how Keys Cafe custom layouts behave when the user switches to a different language layout is not documented]
non_key_surface_coverage: Coverage is unusually broad because Samsung Keyboard is a system app themed by a SYSTEM-WIDE theme package - a Galaxy Theme restyles the lock screen, home screen, dialer, contacts, messages, settings and icons alongside the keyboard, so keyboard theming is a component of whole-device theming rather than a standalone feature. This is the inverse of Gboard and SwiftKey, which theme only their own surface. Within the keyboard, the theme covers the suggestion/prediction bar, the toolbar row, emoji and sticker panels, and key-press pop-ups; Theme Park's 'key-press effect' and Keys Cafe's press animations are explicitly themeable. Clipboard and in-keyboard settings sheets follow the theme's surface colors. Because the keyboard shares One UI's design system, its chrome matches the system automatically in a way third-party keyboards must emulate manually. [uncertain - per-surface coverage is observational; Samsung does not enumerate which keyboard surfaces a theme covers]
sound_haptic_theming: The ONLY one of the three researched keyboards where sound is genuinely part of a theme - a meaningful differentiator. Keys Cafe explicitly bundles SOUNDS alongside colors and animations as part of a keyboard style: coverage describes it as letting you 'add fun colors, animations, or sounds when you press a button', and Samsung's own guidance positions Keys Cafe as customizing 'pre-built themes, animation, colour and sound' together. So a Keys Cafe style is an audio-visual package, not just a skin. Stock Samsung Keyboard settings retain conventional global keypress sound and vibration toggles independent of the visual theme, and Samsung devices also expose system-level touch sound and haptic intensity settings that override or gate the keyboard's own. Underlying APIs are presumably SoundPool/AudioManager plus Vibrator/VibrationEffect, with Samsung's own haptics engine on newer devices. This is the pattern to copy if themed sound matters to your product - and note that it lives in a companion app, not the keyboard itself. [uncertain - the specific audio/haptic APIs are inferred; the exact set of swappable sounds Keys Cafe offers is not documented in the sources reviewed]
platform_apis_frameworks: Android InputMethodService with custom Views and Drawables; Samsung's proprietary theme framework fronted by Galaxy Themes Service / Theme Center (com.samsung.android.themecenter), which installs and applies signed theme APKs system-wide; Android runtime resource overlay (RRO) mechanics for overlay-delivered theming; the Gallery/photo picker for user images; and color extraction (Palette-API-equivalent) inside Theme Park. Good Lock modules (Keys Cafe, Theme Park) are separately installed Galaxy Store apps that hook into Samsung's system apps through Samsung-private interfaces unavailable to third parties. Galaxy Themes Studio is the authoring side, compiling designs to APK without code. Everything here is Samsung-proprietary and Galaxy-exclusive - Samsung explicitly states content produced by Galaxy Themes Studio 'only works on Galaxy smartphones'. None of this is reusable by a third-party keyboard; it is a reference for product shape only. [uncertain - Samsung-private interfaces and the RRO characterization are inferred, not documented]
delivery_installation_pipeline: Four routes, all Samsung-controlled. (1) BUILT-IN - the 5 stock themes ship in the keyboard/One UI itself. (2) GALAXY THEMES STORE - full system themes including keyboard styling, authored in Galaxy Themes Studio, compiled to a signed APK, published only through Galaxy Store (Samsung is explicit that Themes Studio content 'can only be distributed through Galaxy Store'), installed and applied by the Galaxy Themes Service. Paid and free themes are both supported and this is a genuine revenue-sharing designer marketplace. (3) GOOD LOCK MODULES - Keys Cafe and Theme Park are installed from Galaxy Store as separate apps; user creations are stored locally by those apps and applied to the keyboard. Samsung's own support answer for 'change your keyboard background' is literally to install Keys Cafe and Theme Park from Galaxy Store first. (4) COMMUNITY/ROOT (unsupported) - overlay APKs pushed to /system/vendor/overlay with correct permissions, requiring root. GATING IS THE HEADLINE FACT: becoming a Galaxy Themes designer requires an application with at least three complete mockup themes (each covering 6 required screens - Lock, Home, Messages, Dialer, Contacts, Settings - plus redesigns of 8 app icons, submitted as 18 sheets in one PDF), and applications are only accepted during a submission window that opens roughly once every two years, granting a two-year qualification. That is an extraordinarily high barrier compared to SwiftKey's curated-but-first-party gallery or Gboard's absent channel - Samsung runs a closed professional marketplace, not an open one.
permission_store_policy_surface: Android-only and Galaxy-only, so no iOS Full Access considerations apply. Enabling the keyboard uses the standard Android IME enable flow with the usual 'may collect all the text you type' warning; Samsung Keyboard is preinstalled and enabled by default on Galaxy devices, so most users never see that. Theme APKs are installed through Galaxy Store and validated by Samsung signature - the Galaxy Themes Service carries the Samsung certificate, and signature mismatch is a documented cause of install failure, which is the enforcement point. Themes are pure resources rather than executable code, keeping them inside store policy. The designer-approval gate plus store-only distribution means Samsung's content-moderation surface is handled by curation at admission rather than by post-hoc review of user-generated content. For a third-party product the transferable observation is narrow: Samsung's model is only available to Samsung, and its policy posture (closed marketplace, signed packages, curated authors) is the opposite end of the spectrum from an open UGC theme store. [uncertain - signature enforcement details are inferred from APKMirror signature notes and general Samsung theme behavior, not from a published policy document]
memory_performance_budget: No published budget, and no iOS-style hard ceiling since this is Android-only. Samsung Keyboard has a public reputation for being heavier and slower than Gboard - user reports of high RAM usage are common, and One UI 8 coverage is framed around settings changes needed to make the keyboard perform well, which is a soft admission. As a preinstalled system app it is typically resident, so its footprint is persistent rather than on-demand. Theme-specific costs are modest for the dominant color-token model (colors and small drawables, negligible bitmap memory) and rise for the image routes - a Keys Cafe background image or Theme Park per-key images add decoded bitmap cost, and Keys Cafe's key-press animations add per-frame work during typing, which is the more likely source of perceptible input latency than memory. No documented downsampling policy, bitmap cache strategy, or animation frame cap. [uncertain - no memory figures or performance budgets are published for Samsung Keyboard or its theme layer; the animation-cost claim is inference]
untrusted_theme_validation_security: Handled by package-level trust rather than by content validation: themes are signed APKs distributed exclusively through Galaxy Store and installed via the Galaxy Themes Service, so authenticity and integrity ride on Android's package signature verification and Samsung's store curation rather than on parsing and sanitizing an untrusted archive. There is consequently no zip-extraction attack surface in the supported path and no malformed-manifest handling to document - a malformed theme is simply an APK that fails to install. Signature mismatch is a known, documented install-failure mode. The unsupported overlay/root route bypasses all of this by definition. User-supplied images in Keys Cafe and Theme Park are decoded through the platform image decoders with their own hardening. Net: Samsung's answer to untrusted theme content is 'there is no untrusted theme content' - everything is signed and curated. [uncertain - no security documentation exists; this is a structural analysis of the trust model rather than a report of implemented mitigations]
open_source_reference_availability: None. Samsung Keyboard (Honeyboard), Galaxy Themes Service, Theme Park, Keys Cafe, and Galaxy Themes Studio are all closed source, Samsung-proprietary, and Galaxy-exclusive; no theming module, format spec, or SDK is published for the keyboard. Galaxy Themes Studio is a gated GUI tool for approved designers rather than an open format. The only adjacent public material is Samsung Developer's Galaxy Themes documentation (designer-facing, not format-facing) and scattered XDA overlay/theme-tooling threads that work at the APK/RRO level. For a studyable implementation, use an open-source Android keyboard (FlorisBoard, HeliBoard, OpenBoard) or AOSP LatinIME. Samsung's contribution to this research is UX patterns, not code.
authoring_tooling_preview_generation: Three distinct authoring tools at three skill levels, all with live preview - the tiering itself is the lesson. CONSUMER: Theme Park - pick an image, crop it, colors are auto-extracted, a full theme is generated, and a preview screen shows the final look before applying; the keyboard has its own tab where you set base color and style and can assign colors or images to keycaps and text. PROSUMER: Keys Cafe - 'Make your own keyboard' (layout, key add/remove/reorder, height/width/position), 'Style your own keyboard' (design, colors, animations, sounds, and a Gallery icon to set a background image), and, unusually, 'Play keyboard game' - two typing games (Sentence Practice and Word Rain) bundled into the customization app, which is a genuinely novel engagement hook worth noting. PROFESSIONAL: Galaxy Themes Studio - a no-code visual designer that compiles to an APK, with a published Figma template, restricted to approved designers. PREVIEW/THUMBNAIL REQUIREMENTS are the most concrete of any item researched, though they apply to the whole-system theme rather than the keyboard alone: the designer application requires three complete mockup themes at 6 sheets each, 18 sheets total in a single PDF, each mockup covering Lock, Home, Messages, Dialer, Contacts and Settings screens plus redesigns of 8 app icons. If you are planning store-submission requirements for a theme marketplace, that is a real, shipped example of what a strict multi-variant preview requirement looks like.
cross_platform_token_parity: Not applicable in the usual sense and instructive because of it: Samsung Keyboard is Android-only and further restricted to Samsung Galaxy devices, so there is no iOS counterpart and no cross-platform token question. Samsung is explicit that Galaxy Themes Studio content 'only works on Galaxy smartphones'. Themes are not portable to any other keyboard, OEM, or platform, and a Galaxy Theme is a whole-system artifact rather than a keyboard artifact, so it could not be ported even in principle without a target that reproduces One UI's component set. Everything is inherently platform-bound. The relevant lesson is negative: Samsung achieved deep, well-integrated theming precisely BY giving up portability and coupling to a single OEM's system theme framework - a trade a cross-platform third-party keyboard cannot make.
animation_budget: OPEN / WEAKLY DOCUMENTED, but Samsung is the one item here that clearly DOES ship themed animation - which makes its lack of documentation more frustrating rather than less. Keys Cafe explicitly supports 'custom animation effects' and per-key-press color effects as part of a keyboard style, and Theme Park exposes a settable 'key-press effect'. So animation is a first-class part of Samsung's keyboard theming in a way it is not for Gboard (none) or SwiftKey (one first-party theme that crashed iOS). What is entirely undocumented: the animation format (whether these are declared assets, parameterized built-in effects, or bespoke code - most likely a fixed menu of built-in effects rather than an open format), any frame-rate cap, whether animation pauses when the keyboard is idle, and battery/latency impact. There is no evidence of Lottie, GIF, or video backgrounds - the animation appears to be interaction-triggered key-press effects rather than ambient background motion, which is the cheap and sensible subset. Treat as: themed key-press animation is proven shippable on Android in a production OEM keyboard, but Samsung publishes nothing about how it is bounded. Flag for primary investigation if animated theming matters to your product. [uncertain - format, caps, and idle behavior are all unknown; even the 'built-in effects menu rather than open format' reading is inference from the editor's control surface]
